01.json.summary: The story is told by a young wife whose husband is given one year of hard labour in prison. His only crime was serving cool sherbet to some volunteers of the national movement on a hot summer afternoon. In court she feels proud of him, and he smiles at her as he is taken away. That evening she goes to a Congress meeting for the first time, speaks from the stage and takes the satyagraha pledge. She sends telegrams to her father and father-in-law. Both reply angrily: her father-in-law lives on a government pension and her father has a forest department job and expects a promotion, so neither will give her a home in case it costs them with the government. Alone in the empty house, she is frightened to see two secret police men watching it, and keeps a knife by her bed. Then her husband's friend Gyan Babu, a school teacher, arrives with his wife. Mrs Gyanchand is a strong, proud woman who clearly runs her husband. She insists the narrator come to live with them, sends Gyan Babu for tongas, and jokes away her worry about being a burden. In their home the narrator is treated better than a sister. Soon the two police spies appear outside this house too. One evening Gyan Babu comes home upset: the police had complained to the district officer, and the principal of his school wants the woman sent away. His wife is angry that he did not answer at once. She tells him to say he will never send her away, and to resign if the principal insists. When the narrator cries that they should not suffer for her, the wife says that the wife of a man jailed for honouring the nation's volunteers honours their home. Next evening Gyan Babu returns happy. He had resigned; the principal went to the district officer, came back, asked whether Gyan Babu went to political meetings, belonged to Congress or gave it money, and when he said no to all, returned his resignation. The wife hugs the narrator.

02.json.summary: Bhola Mahto, a villager, marries a second time after his first wife dies. His ten-year-old son Raghu now has a hard life. The stepmother, Panna, is beautiful and proud and makes Raghu do all the heavy housework, and Bhola believes everything Panna says against the boy. Eight years later Bhola dies, leaving Panna with four young children: Kedar, Khunnu, Lachhman and the little girl Jhuniya. Panna expects Raghu to take his own wife and leave them, and she even thinks of marrying again rather than live under him. But one evening she finds Raghu playing with the children. He has made them two little carts and pulls them around, and he plans to sell his gold coin to buy a cow so the children can have milk. Panna is ashamed of her doubts. (Part of the text is missing here.) Later Raghu's wife, Mulia, comes to the house. She does not want to share her husband's earnings with his stepmother and half-brothers. She refuses to cook, quarrels over money for the Dussehra fair, and stops eating until the household is divided. Raghu begs her and refuses, because he loves the children. Panna, to save Raghu from grief, says she herself wants to live apart, and she lights a separate stove. The house is divided and a wall goes up in the courtyard. Raghu eats as if at a funeral and feels his dead father is blaming him. Five years pass. Raghu has two sons. Working the land alone, weak and in debt, he grows old at thirty, gets a slow fever and dies. Kedar, now grown and bitter, even refuses to come when Raghu calls for him at the end. Mulia is left alone with two small boys, ashamed and helpless, and the village says God has punished her pride. Kedar quietly takes Mulia's sons as his own and does not want to marry anyone else. Panna sees that Kedar loves Mulia. She tells Mulia she has found a good bride for Kedar, and when Mulia eagerly offers to go and persuade the girl, Panna says the bride is Mulia herself. Mulia's sad, pale face lights up with new joy.

03.json.summary: The narrator, a newspaper editor living alone in the city, says he can never forget his wedding date. He would like a wife at his side, but he fears the other side of family life: fathers carrying crying babies to the doctor, buying flour in the dark, hiding sweets from their children. So he uses all his cleverness to keep his wife in the village. For some time she has begged him to bring her to the city, and he has even stopped going home in the holidays in case she comes back with him. He writes one excuse after another. First he describes the hard, dangerous life of an editor, with police spies and officers who fear him. Next he writes that the city is full of disease and danger: poison in food, motor accidents, mosquitoes and flies. Third, he says friends never leave his house; they borrow his clothes, watch and shoes, eat at his cost and wait for him on payday. Fourth, he writes that city houses are dark, leaky, haunted and full of thieves; one friend tried to steal his pots and another took his fountain pen. She replies that these are only excuses and he must fetch her. Fifth, he says the street hawkers shout so horribly that a neighbour woman fainted. She answers that she is not afraid of jackals and owls in the village, so hawkers will not scare her. At last he tries an excuse he is sure will work: the city is no place for decent women, because bold, beautiful maidservants decked in gold push into homes on any excuse and shame the housewives. Three days later his wife arrives at his door with her three children and an old servant. Taking off her shawl, she asks whether any witch is sitting in the house, and says she will cut the nose of anyone who sets foot there. The narrator realises his last trick has struck his own face.

04.json.summary: After thirty days of fasting in Ramzan, the day of Eid has come, and the whole village is busy getting ready to walk three kos (about six miles) to the Idgah, the open ground for Eid prayers in town. The children are the happiest. Mahmood has twelve paise and Mohsin has fifteen. Hamid, a thin, poor boy of four or five, is happiest of all. His father died of cholera last year and his mother also died, but he has been told that his father has gone to earn money and his mother has gone to Allah to bring him nice things. He lives with his old grandmother Ameena, who sits crying because there is no food in the house for Eid. She is afraid to let him go alone, but he goes with the other boys, with only three paise in his pocket. On the way the boys see big buildings, sweet shops and the police lines, and Mohsin tells tall stories about jinns and dishonest policemen. At the Idgah everyone, rich or poor, prays together in rows. After the prayer the other boys ride the merry-go-round and buy clay toys: Mahmood a soldier, Mohsin a water-carrier, Noorey a lawyer and Sammi a washerwoman. Hamid cannot afford them and says clay toys break easily. The boys buy sweets, and Mohsin teases Hamid by offering him one and then eating it himself. At an iron shop Hamid remembers that his grandmother burns her fingers taking bread off the griddle because she has no tongs. He bargains and buys a pair of tongs (chimta) for three paise. The boys laugh at first, but Hamid argues so well that his tongs are a gun, a brave fighter, the 'Rustam of India', stronger than all their toys, that they agree he has won. They even trade toys for a look at the tongs. Back in the village the other toys soon break: Mohsin's water-carrier falls, Noorey's lawyer falls from his shelf, and Mahmood's soldier loses his legs. When Ameena sees the tongs she first scolds Hamid for buying iron tongs and eating nothing all day. But when he says he bought them because her fingers burn on the griddle, her anger turns to love. She weeps, blesses him again and again, and Hamid cannot understand why she is crying.

05.json.summary: Manhar, a poor office clerk, has been married for three years to Vageshwari (he calls her Bagi), a simple, devoted wife who runs the house, does the hardest work herself and encourages him. Manhar studies detection and writes a book on it that becomes famous, and the government sends him to England to train. Vageshwari stays home to serve his parents. In London Manhar sees that a beautiful, clever wife helps a man rise, and he begins to look down on Vageshwari. He solves several theft cases and courts a young Englishwoman, Jenny Rose, telling her his Indian wife is dead. Jenny flirts with Mr. Coward, private secretary to Lord Barbar, the minister for India, and through him gets Manhar a high post in the Indian secret police. Manhar and Jenny marry and settle in Bombay. He cuts off his family and does not even open Vageshwari's letters. Over two years the marriage goes bad: Jenny lives for parties and plays with men's feelings, and Manhar drinks heavily. When he is ill on a case in Lucknow, she insists on going to Nainital, telling him an English wife is no man's servant and that he married her only for a post. Broken, Manhar resigns, writes to Jenny that he leaves her free and leaves her everything, and drinks hard. When she comes to him he calls her Bagi and does not know her; he has forgotten the last three years. A week later he disappears. He walks back to his village, starving and in rags, to find his family poor. He remembers nothing of England, Jenny or his post, but is now gentle, serves his parents and Vageshwari, and earns a living tracing local thefts. Six months later Jenny, her money spent, arrives to take him to a doctor. Learning that Vageshwari is his wife, she realises he lied to her, attacks him, and pulls a pistol on Vageshwari; Manhar snatches it away. When his mother insults Jenny, she picks the pistol up again to shoot Vageshwari. Manhar steps in front of her, takes the pistol and shoots himself in the chest.

06.json.summary: This story is written as a short play. Mr. Kanooni Kumar, a member of the legislative assembly, sits in his office near a park, surrounded by newspapers and reports, always worrying about the country. Looking out at the park, he finds a problem in everything and decides each one needs a new law. Boys are smoking, so he plans a bill to ban tobacco. Women sit in the park in purdah (covered from head to foot), so he plans a bill to end purdah. A hungry beggar asks him for help; he calls the man a pig and drives him away, then plans a bill to ban begging. A tea seller has no customers, so he plans questions in the assembly about spreading tea drinking. Visitors come. Mrs. Bose, a modern poet, says her husband stops her from going to the hills and to clubs and that she wants a divorce. Mrs. Aiyar complains that her husband forced her to go to the hills against her wish. Kanooni Kumar promises both of them a divorce bill. Mr. Acharya, who runs a hotel with empty rooms, says India will only progress if people live in hotels, and Kanooni Kumar agrees to a law that people earning under 500 rupees must live in hotels. Then he sees a weak, pregnant woman with three small children and plans a birth control bill that would jail parents of more than two children. His wife comes in. He hides his papers and pretends to read a novel. She mockingly proposes her own law: every husband must give half his income to his wife, and men from fifteen to fifty may not leave the house, on pain of prison. He says this is impossible, because law cannot change human nature. She answers that if law can force children into school and fix the age of marriage, it can do this too. She says real reform comes from education and awareness, not from forcing people by law, and that men who cannot give up their own comforts are not fit to reform the country. She leaves, and Kanooni Kumar walks up and down the room, troubled and confused.

07.json.summary: Keshav and Prema are students in the same college class and are deeply in love. Keshav is a Brahmin with modern ideas who rejects caste rules; Prema comes from a Vaishya (trader) family and believes in old customs and in obeying her parents. One evening in Victoria Park, Keshav asks her to marry him against her family's wishes. Prema says she cannot go against her parents, and Keshav leaves, hurt. That night Prema cannot sleep, and she decides she will marry no one but Keshav. The next morning her father, Lalaji, shows her a picture of a young man who came first in the I.C.S. exam. Prema says such men only want power and money, and she brings Keshav's photo to her father. When he learns Keshav is a Brahmin, not from their own caste, he is angry and stops her from going to college, even though her exams are near. Six months pass. Prema is wasting away with grief, so Lalaji decides to accept the marriage, though his wife is strongly against it. He goes to Keshav's father, a bad-tempered, miserly retired government man and a proud high-caste Brahmin. The old Panditji insults Lalaji and sends him away. Then he calls Keshav and threatens to throw him out of the house and give him nothing if he marries a trader's daughter. Keshav loses his courage and says the story is completely false. The next day Prema writes to Keshav that she is ready to face any hardship with him, does not care about his father's money, and invites him to dinner with her parents. He does not come. The next morning his reply arrives: he cannot disobey his father, she should not think him a coward, and she should forget the past. Prema tears up the letter. She tells her mother only that Keshav is unwell, spends the day doing housework, eats dinner with the family and sings at the harmonium late into the night. In the morning she is found dead in her room.

08.json.summary: The narrator sits at home with a few women friends, Padma Devi, Urmila Devi and Shyama Devi, who all work for a national (freedom movement) organisation. They are angry about three leading workers, called only Mr 'K', Mr 'Kh' and Mr 'G'. They say 'K' owes the organisation at least a thousand rupees, 'Kh' spends public money on car rides and parties with friends, and 'G' drinks liquor in secret, even liquor bought from the very shops the women picket. Shyama Devi says she will shame 'G' in a public meeting. The narrator himself was once secretary of this organisation and left after people complained that he gave it too little time, so he is jealous of 'G', who keeps the same post. He quietly pushes the talk along while pretending to defend 'G'. Then another worker, Bhagwati Devi, comes back tired from collecting donations. Her ten-year-old daughter is hungry, and Bhagwati has the house key, so the narrator offers to take the girl home. On the way the girl asks him whether he knows that Mr 'G' drinks. She has heard it from everyone in town, and she also repeats the charges about 'K' wasting public money and 'Kh' riding in cars. She says that people who serve a poor people's organisation should not show off, and that the women feel ashamed when donors throw these charges at them. The narrator does not want to plant hatred and gossip in a simple child's heart. He tells her the town is lying. He reminds her that these three men have each just served a year in jail, opened a hospital and a library, and got the farmers' rent reduced, and that everyone has faults. When she asks once more whether 'G' drinks, he firmly says no, and whoever says so is lying. They reach her house and she goes in. The narrator feels happier about this lie than he has ever felt about telling the truth, because he has kept a pure young heart from falling into the mud of slander.

09.json.summary: The narrator, a writer in Lucknow, meets his old friend Naveen, a lawyer from Agra who loves poetry. Naveen is very upset. His only child, his daughter Kusum, is a modest, clever and well-educated girl. She was married a year ago to a young man in Moradabad, but her husband will not speak to her. She has gone to his house three times and he has ignored her completely. She has written him letters, and he has sent them all back. Now there is talk that he will marry again, and Kusum cries day and night and is wasting away. Naveen asks the narrator to write a moving letter to the husband on Kusum's behalf. The narrator first reads Kusum's five returned letters. In them she begs to know her fault, offers to serve her husband in any hardship, describes standing for hours in his room while he would not look at her, says she has hardly eaten and the doctor fears tuberculosis, asks him only to come to her funeral, and even offers to serve any new wife he may take. In the last letter she says she now understands that a woman is treated as a man's property; she asks for her letters back and offers to return his jewels and clothes. The narrator is angry at the husband and also annoyed at how humbly Kusum begs. He goes to Moradabad. Everyone praises the young man, who is polite and charming. At last the young man admits the reason: he agreed to the marriage hoping Naveen would pay for him to study in England, and when Naveen did not answer his request, he turned away from Kusum. Naveen, who had no idea of this, at once agrees to pay and prepares to send a cheque for a thousand rupees. But Kusum refuses. She says this is like a kidnapper asking for ransom, and that she will take poison if the money is sent. She will not live with such a selfish man. The narrator embraces her with pride. A year later she has not written to her husband or spoken of him, and her face now shows self-respect and independence instead of grief.

10.json.summary: In Tsarist Russia, Ivan, from a rich Moscow family, comes out of Okhotsk jail after fourteen years, very thin but full of burning anger, and gives all his money to the guards. Fifteen years earlier he was a generous, brave student who loved a clever, beautiful fellow student, Helen, and they planned to marry. Helen supported the nationalists, and Ivan joined because of her. A harsh governor, Romanov (Romanaf in the text), came to Ukraine, sent editors to Siberia, had police fire on crowds and declared martial law. Helen decides to kill him: she will win his trust by pretending love, then take him to a park bench at night where Ivan will shoot him. Ivan has doubts but agrees, and Helen asks him to forgive in advance anything she must do. She charms Romanov; she tells Ivan he is not as bad as people say, and police cruelty in the city falls. On the chosen night Helen seems nervous and tries to leave early, but Romanov thanks her for changing his policy. Ivan fires and misses, and is arrested. Helen says she did not know he had become a revolutionary, and at the trial she is the government's witness against him. After fourteen years Ivan goes to Helen, planning to crush her with bitter words for betraying him for pleasure and power. He finds her funeral going on at Romanov's house. When he starts to insult her body, Romanov stops the men dragging him away and tells him Helen confessed everything, never stopped remembering him, and on her deathbed asked that he be told she was guilty and begged his forgiveness. He shows Ivan her peaceful face. Ivan's anger melts; he prays to God to forgive her, helps carry the coffin and weeps at the grave. The next day Romanov finds Ivan there, bowed in prayer and dead.

11.json.summary: Seth Nanakchand is a rich moneylender in a small town. He is hard and has no pity for debtors, but he is very religious: he fasts, feeds Brahmins, bathes in the Jamuna and plans to build a rest house for pilgrims. He has no children. His wife, Kesar, a plump woman who loves fine things, is always afraid of illness and death. Nanakchand has received three letters from a band of robbers. The third one demands 25,000 rupees by evening and says that otherwise they will attack his house that night, openly, in daylight. The Seth is frightened but decides to fight. He has strong doors and rifles, he jokes about teaching Kesar to shoot, and he plans to ask the police for help, because he pays the government ten thousand rupees a year in tax and has often sent gifts to police officers. Just then four constables arrive and say the inspector sent them. Their head constable says the police already know about the letters and that the robbers, twenty of them in disguise, will attack the next day. He advises the Seth to put all his valuables in the government treasury for safe keeping; the Seth will keep the key and get a receipt. The relieved Seth praises the British government's efficiency. The constables load his jewels, gold coins, cash notes, silk saris and shawls into his large car, and the Seth squeezes in with them while Kesar watches from the door. On the road to the police station, five miles away, the head constable asks about his life. The Seth says his father came with almost nothing and he started with three rupees, and that he would gladly escape this world of money and go to pray at a holy place if God allowed it. The head constable says God has sent them to free him from his chains of wealth: they are the same "God's soldiers" who wrote the letters. The Seth is pushed out of the car. As he runs after it begging, the robber throws three rupees out of the window, and the car speeds away with everything he owned.

12.json.summary: The whole story is told by a wife who complains about her husband. To the world he is a kind, polite, generous gentleman, but she says she has never had any comfort from him. He buys goods from small, failing shops because the shopkeepers flatter him, so the wheat is bad, the rice coarse and the ghee mixed with oil. He once gave her gold and a hundred rupees to an old school friend, a goldsmith, and got back an ugly piece that was half copper. His poor friends borrow money and never return it, and guests crowd their tiny house so that she and the children are left without beds and blankets. He hired a useless servant, Ghure, and when she scolded the man, the husband secretly swept the room himself every morning so that Ghure would not be blamed, until she caught him and threw Ghure out. In bitter cold he gave his only coat to the sweeper, who drinks, and he shivered for days until she had a new one made. He never brings her or the children a present. At his office he will not flatter his officers, so he gets no promotions, is given the hardest work, and keeps losing jobs. His rich brother, a tahsildar, controls the family property and never sends them their share, yet the husband will not ask firmly and still praises him. He will not punish the children. Once, when their son Mannu came home late, he went out angrily with a stick but only put his hand gently on the boy's shoulder and told him not to do it again. He plays cards and flies kites with the boys and takes them to fairs, unlike her own strict father. At their daughter's wedding he refused any dowry, ate instead of fasting, and would not sit under the wedding canopy for the giving away of the bride, then sulked for months until she made peace. Yet at the end she admits that, with all these faults, she cannot bear to be apart from him even for a moment. If he is late she is frightened. She would not exchange him for the cleverest, richest or most handsome man, because over the years they have fitted together like the worn parts of a machine.

13.json.summary: The story is told almost entirely as a conversation, like a short play. A widowed mother complains to her son, a tired office clerk, about his young wife: she is rude, sleeps late, reads novels while the old mother cooks, will not press her mother-in-law's feet, does not get up or touch the feet of visiting neighbourhood women, and neglects her baby. The mother blames the son for spoiling her. The son defends his wife at every point. Service to his mother is his own duty, not his wife's; husband and wife are equal; respect should go only to those who deserve it, and the visiting women are gossips; the wife grew up in a rich home with a cook, and the family hid its own poverty at the wedding, so now they must cover it with kindness. A house becomes a girl's own only when her mother-in-law treats her like a daughter. Suddenly the wife walks in. She tells her husband that a man who listens to his wife being insulted is not fit to be a husband; in her father's house he is honoured, while here she is treated like a servant. She will learn with love, not by force. The mother, hurt that her son listens to his wife, leaves in tears. The wife calls this a woman's jealousy and says she will never become a mother-in-law herself. Then the husband cleverly tells her that his mother has changed: he claims she now worries the wife may catch cold getting up early, no longer wants her to press feet or cook, wants to hire a cook and hand her the household money. None of this was said in the talk we heard. The delighted wife at once decides to get up early, touch the old women's feet, cook until he gets a pay rise, press her mother-in-law's feet, spend less and leave the money with the mother. She goes off happily to cook dinner.

14.json.summary: Muliya is a very beautiful young woman from a poor Chamar (low-caste) family, married to Mahavir, who drives an ekka (a one-horse cart). Many young men in the village admire her, but she never looks at any of them. One morning, while she is going to cut grass, Chainsingh, a young Thakur (high-caste landowner), grabs her hand and begs her for pity. She angrily threatens to scream, and he lets her go in shame. She cries on the way but tells no one, because she fears Mahavir would kill the Thakur. The next day she does not want to go out alone, but her mother-in-law scolds her, so she goes by another path and starts cutting grass in a green field. Chainsingh finds her again, but this time he stands at a distance and says he is sorry, that he has wept since that day, and that he only wants her kindness. Muliya asks him boldly: would he not want to kill a man who spoke like this to his own wife? He comes to her only because she is a poor, low-caste woman whom he thinks he can win cheaply. Her husband loves only her and would care for her even if she went blind, and she will never cheat him. Her words change Chainsingh completely. He becomes gentle and kind with the old woman watering his field and with the labourers he used to beat. One day he rides to the court in Mahavir's ekka and learns that buses (lorries) have taken away Mahavir's business, so Muliya now sells grass in town every day. At the court Chainsingh sees Muliya, dressed in a pink sari, bargaining and laughing with the cart drivers, and then taking money from a young lawyer in a carriage. He stands there stunned. On the way back he offers Mahavir a rupee a day to be ready with his ekka whenever needed, so that his wife need not go to the market, and asks him not to tell Muliya. Some days later Muliya meets Chainsingh at the place where he once held her arm. She says she no longer sells grass and thanks him: by helping them he has kept the honour of the arm he once held, and he has saved her, because poverty makes people do anything. She hopes he did not think badly of her, and he says he never did.

15.json.summary: Chandraprakash has just passed his B.A. when his father dies, leaving no money and a young, educated wife, Champa, who likes nice things. He takes a thirty-rupee tuition job teaching Virendra (Biru), the slow son of Thakur Sahib. The Thakur and his wife treat Prakash like a son, give him a free house joined to theirs, and ask his advice on everything. When Biru's marriage is fixed, they put Prakash in charge of the whole wedding. He is honest with their money, but the day he buys five thousand rupees of jewellery for the bride, his mind becomes restless. Champa cries that she has not even a decent sari for the wedding. That night Prakash climbs the low wall between the two roofs and steals the jewel box. Next morning he blames the servants, but footprints on the wall show the thief came from his side. Prakash blames his own carelessness and moves out at once; the Thakur only admires him more and keeps paying his rent. Prakash keeps the jewels in a locked box and says it holds old books. Champa grows suspicious, opens it with a key bought from a pedlar, recognises the jewels, and is filled with shame. She says nothing, but her love fades and they quarrel often. Months later Prakash wants a bank post that needs a ten-thousand-rupee cash deposit, and the Thakur offers to pay it. Champa reminds Prakash of all the Thakur's kindness and says one should be ready to die for such a man. Her words fill him with guilt. When he gets the job, he invites the Thakur's family to a feast and makes them stay the night. At midnight he takes Biru's keys, carries the jewel box back and leaves it under the Thakur's bed. Next day the Thakur happily says the jewels have returned untouched and calls it a miracle. Prakash says it must be the result of his prayers. Hearing the news, Champa hugs Prakash and cries, as if a lost husband had come home, and says she will feed a thousand poor people. Prakash also weeps.

16.json.summary: The story is told only through a quick, angry conversation between two sisters, Neela and Meena. Neela asks Meena why she wrote a letter to a certain man, the same man who insulted Neela and spread her name around in every street. Meena first says she never wrote to anyone. Then Neela seems to smile, and Meena gets angry about the smile. The two quarrel, calling each other names and accusing each other of jealousy. In the heat of the fight Meena admits everything: she did write to him, she met him in the park and talked with him, he has given her a wristwatch, and she says she does not care about marriage rituals because love is enough for her. She says Neela is just jealous. Neela then explains why she smiled: the same man played the same trick on her. He used to put his head on her feet and cry, saying he would die or take poison if she did not love him. Meena is shocked, because he says exactly the same words to her. Neela calls him a skilled hunter who scatters grain to catch birds, and warns that he will betray Meena and talk about her the same way. The story ends with Meena holding her head in her hands, lost in worry.

17.json.summary: In Bombay, Kavasji runs a newspaper and earns fame but little money, while his friend Shapurji, a cotton broker, earns wealth and respect. Kavasji's wife Gulshan quarrels with him constantly and asks why he married her if he could not feed her. Shapurji's wife Shirin is gentle and sweet, and Kavasji often visits her, secretly wishing she were his wife. One morning he finds Shirin in tears. For months Shapurji has spent his nights away; money has not made her happy and she can bear it no longer. She asks Kavasji to talk to him. Shapurji arrives, admits he spent the night with Miss Gauhar, and says a man may enjoy himself but a wife has no such right. Kavasji pretends to agree, then tells him Shirin is full of rebellious ideas. Shapurji is angry but sure she will only complain and be easy to win back. A few days later, with Gulshan gone off in anger to her parents, Kavasji meets Shirin in a park. She says she has left Shapurji for good and will live with Kavasji if he gives her a home; he promises to divorce Gulshan. But while fetching a taxi he grows afraid that a woman used to luxury will soon hate his poor cottage and plain food. He stops Shapurji's passing car and begs him to take Shirin home, but Shapurji refuses to go and coax her. Standing there confused, Kavasji now sees Gulshan's good side: she quarrels, but feeds him on time, mends his clothes and is happy with little. Just then Gulshan arrives, worried after a bad dream about him. He is forced to tell her about Shirin and Shapurji, hiding his own part, but she guesses the truth. She says Shirin should stay in her husband's house, enjoy his money and live as freely as he does. When Kavasji points out that she too loves money, Gulshan says that is the curse of life: we run after what ruins us. If he ever got rich he would become like Shapurji, and she admits she would then follow her own advice.

18.json.summary: Booti, a woman of the Ahir (cowherd) caste, became a widow five years ago while still young. She could have married again, as her community allows, but she wanted to be known as a faithful widow. Her life is hard and she has become bitter, and she takes her anger out on her children, mostly on her elder son Mohan, who is sixteen. Her other children are Sohan, a lazy younger boy, and a little girl, Maina. Booti also dislikes women who wear jewellery and make-up. One evening she scolds Mohan for secretly laughing and talking with Rupiya, a young girl of the neighbourhood, and for buying her paan (betel leaf) and paying to dye her clothes. When Mohan says it is the age for such pleasures, Booti feels he is calling her old. Mohan says he has promised to marry Rupiya, but Booti says she will throw Rupiya out with a broom. Mohan refuses to eat. That night Rupiya comes to him secretly, and her sweet words fill him with love. The next morning Mohan is full of happiness and treats everyone kindly. He gives Sohan money to have his dhoti washed, gives Maina two paise for her doll's wedding, and takes the heavy load of cow-dung from his mother's head. That day he also brings his mother paan, a small paan box and some sweets. Booti's hard heart softens. She shares the sweets with her children, enjoys the paan, and becomes friendly with her neighbours. When she goes to see the sick baby of a neighbour, Dhaniya, she learns that Rupiya has been helping Dhaniya all day and sat up all night with the child. Booti sees that Rupiya is kind as well as pretty, and her dislike turns to love. After that Rupiya visits Booti every day, and Booti even has Mohan buy her a good sari. One day Booti asks Rupiya, half in fun, if she should marry her to Mohan, and Rupiya blushes. When Mohan returns that day, Booti tells him to gather some money, because she is talking with Rupa about his marriage.

19.json.summary: The story is told by a shopkeeper. For several days his home has been full of quarrels. His mother and his wife are not speaking, no one has eaten, and even the children are sad and confused. The fight began over the gifts to be sent to his sister's house for the Teej festival. His mother wanted to send saris, toys and sweets, but his wife felt the list was too long, since the shop earns very little and the family has already cut its spending. The quarrel grew into bitter words. The narrator secretly agrees with his wife, but he is afraid to take either side. It is the evening of Janmashtami, Krishna's birthday, and the whole town is celebrating, but his house is dark. When he asks why no lamp is lit, his wife answers rudely, his mother adds a sharp remark, and he and his wife exchange angry words. He sits alone in a dark room, cursing the day he married. His friend Pandit Jaidev comes calling. The narrator first does not answer, then says he has a headache, but Jaidev tickles him until he agrees to come and see the jhanki (the decorated display of Krishna) at the temple of Seth Ghurelal. Ghurelal was a famous miser who gave all his wealth to religion after a beggar died of hunger at his door. The temple is crowded and full of electric lights and jewels. The narrator does not like the showy display, but in the courtyard Kelkarji and his students begin to play music, and the music carries him in his mind to Krishna on the bank of the Yamuna. Then a young student sings a dhrupad song. The narrator cannot follow the words, but the voice fills him with love. He forgives his dead younger brother, who once fought with him and ran away to Rangoon with the family's money. He feels love even for his enemies. He remembers his wife Vidya as she looked on their wedding night ten years ago and longs to fall at her feet and cry, and he feels as if his mother has taken him in her lap. When the singing ends and people leave, he keeps sitting, lost in these feelings, until Jaidev calls out to ask if he is coming or will sit there all night.

20.json.summary: Seth Khubchand, a rich Bombay mill owner, cares only about money; he sends costly Christmas gifts to officials and keeps a temple only for show. Though his Swadeshi mill made a profit of ten lakh rupees, he cuts the workers' wages, and they go on strike. Their leader is a thin young man, Gopinath. When Khubchand arrives at the mill, he has the police beat the workers, and when Gopinath walks towards him to speak, he shoots him. The angry workers trap Khubchand on top of the cotton bales and are about to set them on fire, but the wounded Gopinath comes forward and begs them to go home and let the Seth leave. They obey. Khubchand drives away, and Gopinath falls dead. Ashamed, Khubchand tells his pious wife Pramila everything. When a huge crowd carrying Gopinath's body attacks his house, he gives himself up so that no more lives are lost. He confesses in court and is sentenced to fourteen years of transportation (kala pani). His wealth is lost, Pramila gives up her jewels, and seven months later she gives birth to a son, Krishnachandra. The boy grows up to look exactly like Gopinath. He finds Gopinath's poor widow, old mother and daughter Binni, who work in the same mill, and helps them, which worries Pramila. After fifteen years Khubchand returns, old and broken but now deeply devoted to God, and is overjoyed to find a son who looks like the man he killed; he believes Gopinath has been reborn as his son. A week later Binni calls Krishnachandra because the workers want him to talk to the cruel mill manager about harsh fines. The manager refuses, a strike begins, armed guards fire, and Krishnachandra falls first. Khubchand runs there, holds his son's body, tells the workers he is proud of his brave son and leads them into the office. He makes the directors agree to end the fines. Pramila cannot accept this as God's will and dies of grief that night. Three years later, Khubchand lives to serve the workers' families, who have built a small temple. At the Krishna festival, he sees both Krishnachandra and Gopinath in the image of child Krishna, and feels God's mercy has guided his whole life.

21.json.summary: The story is set during the freedom movement, when Congress volunteers stop shops from selling foreign cloth. Chhakaudilal owns a very small cloth shop. He lives on it with his old mother, his sick wife Amba and five children. When the movement began he let the Congress put a seal on his foreign cloth and bought a little Indian cloth on credit, but nobody wanted it and he sold almost nothing. He went into debt and sold the family's jewellery, and now his wife badly needs a good doctor. When a buyer offered to take ten rupees of foreign cloth, he secretly broke the seal and sold it at cost. Amba was angry: she said she would rather die than be the cause of such shame, and she refused to see any doctor. In despair Chhakaudi threw the ten rupees into the well. A neighbouring shopkeeper reports him. A woman volunteer comes with two helpers to picket his shop. He begs her pardon, but she says he must pay a fine. In anger he threatens to go to the police, and the crowd turns against him. The boycott committee fines him 101 rupees. He cannot pay. He secretly sells his cloth cheaply at home, but volunteers find out and start picketing his house and holding a mock mourning at his door. Amba sends him to the Congress office to ask for 25 rupees a month in exchange for burning his cloth. The Congress president does not believe he is poor and says that if one man is let off, many others will break their seals too. Chhakaudi says the Congress, like the police, is sucking the blood of the poor, and even offers to work for them for 25 rupees a month, but the president refuses. At home Amba first wants to go and lie in front of the Congress office and die there with her hungry children to shame them. But when Chhakaudi repeats the president's reasons, she thinks and agrees that he is right. She tells her husband to mortgage their house to pay the fine and never to sell foreign cloth again, whatever happens to her or the children, because the country matters more. Chhakaudi, annoyed with her but knowing she will not change her mind, goes to the moneylender.

22.json.summary: Timur, the Tatar conqueror, has defeated the Turks at Constantinople. Seventy thousand Turkish soldiers are dead, and the Turkish general Yazdani stands before him with a hundred thousand captured men. Yazdani says he wants life with honour, or death. Timur calls the Turks' life of pleasure a sin against Islam, and his soldiers start killing the prisoners. Then a handsome young officer behind Yazdani steps forward and boldly scolds Timur: does Islam allow killing brave Muslims in chains whose only crime was defending their caliph and country? Did Timur fight for God or for his own greed? Timur, who has never heard such fearless words, is deeply moved. He stops the killing, frees the prisoners, learns the young man's name is Habib, weeps as he tells his own cruel life, and begs Habib to become his chief minister (wazir). In fact Habib is Yazdani's daughter, Ummatul Habib. Raised like a son, she learned riding and weapons as well as philosophy, chose Islam after her own study, served as an army officer, and refused all marriage offers to keep her freedom. Her parents fear for her, but she accepts, hoping to make Timur more humane. In Samarkand she becomes the real ruler and everyone loves her fairness. Timur begs her to live in his palace; she refuses, saying a man's greatest enemy is pride. When the Christians of Istakhar rebel against the tax on non-Muslims (jizya) and bans on church bells and wine, Habib goes there. Timur tells her he loves her more than any woman he has known. She abolishes the tax and the bans; the local Muslims and royal troops besiege her in the fort and tell Timur she has rebelled. Timur instead declares that Habib is the real master and that church bells are no sin. He arrives under a white flag, praises her, confirms the Christians' rights and even returns their self-rule. That night he asks her to guard his empire. She agrees, then asks what if Habib were an unmarried girl. He says she would be queen of his heart too, and that he knew from her first look. Habib became known as Timur's queen, Hamida.

23.json.summary: (The text given here starts in the middle of the story.) Mangal is a poor orphan boy of the sweeper (bhangi) caste, an untouchable group. He lives at the door of Babu Maheshnath's house and eats the leftover food from the family's plates. His only friend is a dog named Tommy. One day Mangal plays with Maheshnath's spoiled eight-year-old son Suresh and two other boys. Suresh tries to ride Mangal like a horse without giving him a turn. Mangal slips from under him and Suresh falls and cries. Suresh tells his mother that Mangal touched him. She does not beat Mangal, because touching him even with a stick would mean she had to bathe, but she curses him and orders him never to come to her door again. Mangal picks up his clay bowls and his piece of sacking and goes away crying to the ruined hut where he once lived. Tommy follows him. As evening comes, hunger grows stronger than shame. Mangal and Tommy talk, the dog in his own way, and decide to go back and hide near the house to see if anyone calls for Mangal. They stand in the dark. Tommy creeps inside. Mangal hears the servants saying they are glad he is gone, because they no longer have to see a sweeper's face in the morning. No one calls his name. As he is about to leave sadly, a servant comes out carrying the leftovers from the family's plates to throw away. He sees Mangal and gives him the food on a leaf plate. Mangal and Tommy eat it together under a neem tree. Mangal strokes the dog and says that hunger is like this. Then he remembers that his own mother nursed and raised Suresh. People say no one can ever repay the price of a mother's milk, he says, and this is the price he is getting for that milk. Tommy wags his tail each time.

24.json.summary: The story opens by saying the donkey is called a fool only because it is so patient, and the ox is its younger brother. The farmer Jhuri owns two fine oxen, Hira and Moti, who are like brothers: they talk without words, lick each other and share every load. Jhuri sends them to his in-laws' village with his wife's brother, Gaya. Thinking they have been sold, they refuse to eat, break their ropes at night and walk home. Jhuri hugs them and the children cheer, but Jhuri's wife calls them ungrateful and gives them only dry straw. Gaya takes them back, ties them with thick ropes, beats them and feeds them dry straw. When he hits Hira on the nose, Moti runs off and breaks the plough. Moti wants to fight the men, but Hira says it is not their way. Their only kindness comes from Gaya's motherless little daughter, beaten by her stepmother, who brings them two rotis each night. When she hears the family plans to put rings through their noses, she unties them and then shouts that they are running away, so she will not be blamed. Lost, the oxen eat peas in a field. A huge bull attacks; they fight it together from both sides until it flees, and Hira will not let Moti strike the fallen enemy. Moti then gets stuck in the mud of another field and is caught, and Hira returns to share his fate. In the cattle pound no animal is fed. Hira breaks part of the mud wall and is beaten and tied up. Moti finishes the job so the horses, goats and buffaloes escape, even pushes out two frightened donkeys, then stays beside his friend. After a week without food, the weak oxen are auctioned to a harsh, bearded butcher. On the road they recognise the way home and run to Jhuri's door. When the butcher tries to take them, Moti chases him out of the village. The oxen get full troughs of good feed, and Jhuri's wife kisses their foreheads.

25.json.summary: Mani lost her father at five; at sixteen she was married, but within a year her mother and husband both died. The young widow moves in with her uncle Vanshidhar. She does all the housework, yet her uncle, aunt and cousin Lalita treat her badly. Only her cousin Gokul, a student, is kind, though too afraid of his mother to defend her openly. On the night of Lalita's wedding, Mani goes in smiling to see the bride and her aunt drives her out like a dog. Hurt, Mani goes upstairs to hang herself from the ceiling fan. Gokul's close friend Indranath, a wedding guest, cuts the rope and tells her that someone loves her more than his own life. Gokul at first suspects Indranath, but Indranath says he wants to marry Mani; her being a widow is no fault in his eyes. After much shyness Mani says yes. Telling his mother that Indranath's family needs help with a function, Gokul takes Mani there, and the two are married by Vedic rites. When Gokul tells his mother the truth, she abuses him and Mani so cruelly that he leaves home and disappears. Indranath takes a job in Bombay and goes ahead; his mother is to follow with Mani. Vanshidhar searches for his son and blames Mani. She writes him a gentle letter of apology. As she is about to leave by train, he comes to the station, refuses to let her touch his feet, and before a crowd curses her as a shameless woman whose death would lighten the earth. On the train Mani decides she will not burden Indranath with her disgrace. At night, while her mother-in-law sleeps, she throws herself from the train; her body is found near Lalpur. Indranath performs her last rites, finds Gokul at the station, and visits Vanshidhar's house. He gives Gokul's mother Mani's farewell letter to her husband, thanking him for his kindness and asking him not to grieve. The mother weeps, and Vanshidhar stands silent on the veranda, as if Mani stood before him in shame.

26.json.summary: Lala Dagamal, a rich merchant of about forty-five, has long neglected his wife Lila, mother of his seven children, who at forty is treated as old. He mocks her when she dresses up, while he dyes his hair and takes tonics to stay young. When Lila is ill with fever she begs him to come home early; he promises eleven o'clock but goes to hear a dancing girl and returns at two. The illness kills her. Dagamal makes a great show of mourning, with scholarships in her name and a grand funeral feast, but six months later, urged by friends, he marries again. His young new wife, Asha, comes from a poor home. He buys a new car, furniture, a radio, jewels and silk saris, and acts young, pressing her to go to the cinema and on river trips. Asha shows no interest, calls him the respectful 'aap', says obeying him is her duty, will not wear the jewels, and prefers to busy herself in the kitchen. The old cook falls ill and sends his son Jugal, a clumsy youth of seventeen. Asha teaches him to cook. He is simple and open, jokes with her, asks for her photo and for good clothes, and she laughs more with him than ever before. When Dagamal calls her to see flower pots he has bought, she answers him sharply and stays at the stove. One day she dresses in all her jewels. Dagamal is thrilled, and when she complains of a pain in her chest he believes his tonic pills have made him young again and boasts about it to his friends. Meanwhile Jugal tells Asha she looks beautiful and that her husband looks like her father; married to a woman of fifty, he says, he would run away or take poison. Asha pretends to be angry but cannot hide her sadness, saying it is fate. Her veil slips from her head. Hearing her husband's car, she pulls it back and hurries to her room, telling Jugal to come after the Lala has eaten and left.

27.json.summary: The narrator is the son of a poor clerk and studies in Allahabad (Prayag) with Ishwari, the son of a big landlord. The two friends often argue: the narrator calls landlords bloodsuckers, while Ishwari defends them weakly but never loses his temper. Ishwari is polite to friends but harsh with servants. For the Dussehra holidays the narrator has no money to go home, so he accepts Ishwari's invitation to his village near Moradabad. Ishwari warns him not to criticise landlords there. They travel second class for the first time in the narrator's life. At the station, Ishwari's men, Riyasat Ali and Ramharakh, look down on the plainly dressed narrator, so Ishwari tells them a big lie: his friend is a rich prince with a large estate who wears only khadi because he is a follower of Mahatma Gandhi. Everyone in Ishwari's fort-like home now treats the narrator with great respect, calling him Kunwar Sahib. Soon he enjoys it: servants wash his feet, press his legs and fan him, and the days pass in boating, hunting and chess instead of study. He grows more demanding than Ishwari himself. He scolds a servant for being late to make his bed, and shouts at Riyasat Ali for not lighting a lamp, though the matches were right there. A villager, Thakur, a Gandhi follower, asks him whether landlords will lose their land under self-rule; the narrator boasts that he will give his own lands to his tenants and promises to make Thakur his driver. On the way back the train is crowded, and they must travel third class. A poor man with a big bundle on his back keeps standing near the door by the narrator's face to get some air. The narrator loses his temper, pushes him and slaps him several times. The whole carriage turns on him, saying that if he is so delicate he should travel first class, and asking whether being rich makes a man lose his humanity. Ishwari says to him in English, 'What an idiot you are, Bir!' The narrator feels his intoxication of borrowed power begin to wear off.

28.json.summary: Neur is a short, strong labourer over fifty who still works harder than young men. His wife Budhiya does no work; she smokes on her cot, dresses up and quarrels with the village. The other workers mock her, but Neur loves her; since their daughter died she has grown weaker, so he cooks and fetches water for her. Budhiya keeps him happy with sweet words, and he works day and night to save a little so she will never have to beg if he dies first. A wandering sadhu sets up his fire under the pipal tree in front of Neur's hut. The village serves him, and simple Neur becomes his most devoted follower. One night the sadhu says God, not Neur, looks after his wife, and offers a miracle: silver placed in a pot in his fire will turn to gold coins by morning. Neur must tell no one. Neur borrows fifty rupees from trusting villagers, adds his own twenty-five, and tricks Budhiya into soaking her silver jewellery in a pot of sour liquid to clean it. At night he takes the pot to the sadhu. In the morning the sadhu and pot are gone. Budhiya cries and curses him, and Neur runs away across the fields in shame. Three months later Neur is himself posing as a sadhu on a hill by the Dhasan river near Kashipur in Jhansi district, while missing home and Budhiya. A young woman, left by her husband after she quarrelled with his mother, asks him to win her husband back. He says it needs a costly ritual, and that night she lays her box of gold jewellery at his feet. This is the chance he has waited for, but he cannot take it. Weeping, he tells her to take it back, saying he was only testing her. He bathes and leaves, feeling free. Reaching his village, he learns Budhiya died three days after he left, cursing him to the end. From that day Neur never speaks, cries or laughs. He sits silently under a tree by the road, taking whatever travellers give. When plague empties the village he stays, and he still sits there, still and lifeless.

29.json.summary: In the early days of Islam in Mecca, Hazrat Muhammad has few followers. His daughter Zainab is married to Abul-Aas, an honest and hard-working trader who does not care for religion. Zainab has secretly come to believe in Islam but hides it, because the Quraish, her husband's powerful tribe, hate the new faith and do not accept mixed marriages. One hot afternoon, while Muhammad and his wife Khadija sit worried about the attacks on Muslims, Zainab arrives alone and asks her father to take her into the faith. He warns her that she may lose her husband, but she says she will not let any person come between her and God, and hopes Abul-Aas will one day believe. The next day she accepts Islam in the mosque. The Quraish are angry, and their leader Abu Sufiyan tells Abul-Aas to divorce her. Abul-Aas refuses: he will not become Muslim, but he will not leave his wife or interfere with her faith, even if he is thrown out of his community. He goes to Muhammad, promises never to force Zainab to change her faith or divorce her, and takes her home. Khadija gives her a precious necklace of Yemeni rubies. As attacks increase, the Muslims move from Mecca to Medina. War follows; Abul-Aas fights against the Muslims, and Zainab goes to care for wounded Muslims. The Muslims win, and Abul-Aas is captured. Zainab sends Khadija's necklace as ransom. Abu Bakr and Zaid say the ransom should be Zainab herself, and Abul-Aas proudly accepts rather than live on their kindness. For three years Zainab lives in Medina with honour but in sorrow, and Abul-Aas, refusing to remarry, buries himself in trade. Then Zaid's men attack his caravan and capture him again. Muhammad will not judge his own son-in-law, fearing bias, and even when Zainab pleads, he says a judge must be free of love and hate. His companions, moved by this, free Abul-Aas with all his goods. Deeply touched by this fairness, Abul-Aas settles his accounts in Mecca, returns everyone's goods, pays his debts and comes to Muhammad as a follower. Zainab's wish is fulfilled.

30.json.summary: Halku is a poor farmer. He has saved three rupees, a little at a time from his wages, to buy a blanket for the cold winter nights when he must guard his crop in the field. But Sahna, to whom he owes rent, comes to collect money. His wife Munni refuses at first, says the debt never ends, and begs him to give up farming and work only for wages. In the end she gives him the three rupees, and he hands them over with a heavy heart. On a freezing night in the month of Poos, Halku lies in his field under a small shelter of sugar cane leaves, with only an old thin sheet. His dog Jabra lies shivering under the cot. Neither can sleep. Halku smokes pipe after pipe and talks to the dog. At last he takes Jabra in his lap and holds him close for warmth, and feels a happiness he has not felt for months. Later, unable to bear the cold, he goes to a nearby mango grove, gathers a big pile of dry leaves and lights a fire. Warm at last, he feels he has beaten the cold, and he even jumps over the fire for fun. When the leaves have burnt down, he sits by the warm ashes and begins to feel lazy. A herd of nilgai (wild antelope) comes into his field and begins eating the ripe crop. Jabra barks and runs at them. Halku hears them, shouts, and gets up once, but a cutting cold wind sends him back to the ashes. He lies down there and falls asleep. In the morning Munni wakes him: the whole field has been eaten and trampled. Halku lies that he had a terrible stomach ache. They find Jabra lying on his back under the shelter as if dead. Munni is sad and says they will now have to work for wages to pay the land tax. But Halku is happy, and says that at least he will not have to sleep out here in the cold at night.

31.json.summary: The narrator, a boy of nine, lives in a school hostel with his elder brother, who is fourteen. The brother is five years older but only three classes ahead, because he takes two or three years to pass each class. He sits with his books all day, though he often just draws animals or writes the same words again and again. The younger boy hates study and runs off to play whenever he can. Each time he returns, his brother asks 'Where were you?' and gives him a long, stinging lecture about how hard English is and how he is wasting their father's money. The boy cries, makes a strict timetable with no play, and breaks it the first day. At the yearly exam the elder brother fails and the younger one comes first. The boy grows bold, but his brother gives him a huge lecture on pride, citing Ravan and Satan, calling his success luck, and describing the horrors of algebra, geometry, the many English kings named Henry, and silly essays. The next year the same thing happens: the younger boy comes first without much work, while the elder, who studied day and night, fails again, and both brothers cry. Now only one class separates them. The elder brother scolds less, and the younger boy almost stops studying and secretly flies kites. One evening the elder brother catches him chasing a cut kite with street boys. He says that even if the younger boy passes him at school, he will always be five years older and wiser in life, just as their unschooled parents know more about running a home than they do. The boy feels small and agrees with tears. The elder brother hugs him and admits he too longs to fly kites but must set an example. Just then a cut kite floats past. The tall elder brother jumps, catches its string, and runs towards the hostel, with the younger boy running behind.

32.json.summary: The narrator is an educated, well-off man. His servant Gangu is a proud, uneducated Brahmin who never salutes him and keeps apart from the other servants. One morning Gangu humbly asks to leave his job: he wants to marry Gomti Devi, a widow just thrown out of the widows' home. The home had married her off three times, and each time she ran away within weeks; now she lives alone nearby and is the talk of the local idlers. Gangu says people have defamed her; her husbands gave her no love, and no woman stays where there is no love. He adds that she has fits when she talks wildly and faints. The narrator thinks him a fool and accepts his resignation. Gangu marries Gomti, rents a small house and sells chaat (spicy snacks). For five months he looks content and self-respecting, and the narrator feels secretly jealous. Then he hears Gomti has run away, and is pleased. Gangu, in tears, tells him she took nothing, not even her own things; she was a blessing to him and he must have failed her. He sets off to search for her. A month later Gangu appears before the narrator, overjoyed, holding a baby boy. He found Gomti in the women's hospital in Lucknow and brought her home. The narrator mocks him: the boy was born only six months after the wedding. Gangu laughs and says that was exactly why Gomti ran away. He had told her he loved her even more than before and that the child was his own: if you take a field that is already sown, you do not reject its crop because someone else sowed it. Moved to tears, the narrator takes the baby in his arms and kisses him. When Gangu calls him a good man, he says he is good only on the surface and mean at heart, while the real goodness is Gangu's. Holding the child, he goes with Gangu to meet Gomti.

33.json.summary: When Pandit Ayodhyanath dies, he leaves a pakka house, two gardens, jewellery and twenty thousand rupees in cash. His widow Phoolmati has four grown sons and one unmarried daughter, Kumud. The sons are Kamtanath, a clerk; Umanath, a new doctor; Dayanath, who writes for magazines; and Sitanath, a bright student. For forty years Phoolmati has run the house, and nothing was done without her word. But at the feast on the thirteenth day after the death, the sons cut the amounts of flour and ghee she had ordered, and the eldest daughter-in-law pays the bills without asking her. The feast goes badly: there is no salt, no cold water, and then a dead mouse is found in the food, so the guests get up and leave. Phoolmati scolds her sons, but Kamtanath only laughs at her old ideas. Two months later the brothers plan Kumud's marriage. Their father had agreed to marry her to the son of Pandit Murarilal for a dowry of five thousand rupees, but the brothers each want their share of the money for their own plans. Only Sitanath offers his share, and Kamtanath talks him out of it. They decide on Pandit Deendayal, a man over forty who will take no dowry. Fearing that their mother will use her jewellery for Kumud, Umanath and Dayanath trick her: they say Dayanath must pay five thousand rupees as bail for an article or go to jail, and she gives them all her jewels. When she still insists that Kumud should marry Murarilal's son, Kamtanath and Umanath tell her that by law the property now belongs to the sons and a mother has a right only to food and clothing. Broken, Phoolmati decides to stay in the house for the sake of the family's name, but now as a servant. She sweeps, cooks and does all the work, and takes no part in any decision. Kumud is married to Deendayal. As she leaves, she gives back to her mother the little money and jewellery Phoolmati tries to give her. A year passes. The sons do well and then badly, but Phoolmati feels nothing and works like an animal. One rainy day, when the maid is ill, she goes to the flooded Ganga to bring drinking water for Kamtanath. Her foot slips and the waves pull her under. People on the bank say it was the widow of rich Ayodhyanath, who had many earning sons, but it was her fate to suffer.

34.json.summary: Early one October morning a beautiful young woman lies fast asleep on a bench beside a path in Gandhi Park. Everyone who passes stops for a moment to look. Two young men, Vasant and Hashim, are running there to train for a race. Hashim is sure she is a prostitute who has slept there after a night of drinking, or is showing off her beauty on purpose. Vasant notes the sindoor (red mark of a married woman) in her hair and thinks she is a respectable wife who may have quarrelled with her husband. Hashim wants to wake her and make friends, but Vasant says it would be rude to speak to a respectable woman. They bet ten rupees each on who is right. Next come two old men, a lawyer and a doctor, both with false teeth and glasses. They talk about the shamelessness of modern girls and also about their own lost youth. They joke about tonics and 'monkey-gland' treatments to feel young again, and one jokes about marrying the girl. He says his own son once threatened him with a gun when he spoke of marrying again. Then they walk off to their clients. Then an older lady and a young woman named Monu arrive by car. The older lady calls the sleeper shameless and says such women make men refuse freedom to women. Monu argues that women show off their freedom because in their hearts they know they are not free. Finally Monu goes and gently wakes the sleeper. The young woman explains that she suffers from dizzy spells. She came to the park for fresh air, felt dizzy, sat on the bench and lost consciousness. She says Doctor Shyamnath is her father-in-law, and that her husband is his son Vasantlal, though her gauna (the ceremony after which a bride goes to live with her husband) has not yet taken place, so they have never really met. Monu tells her that both the doctor and Vasantlal have just passed by, and that she knows Vasantlal from the university. The young woman asks her not to call anyone. Monu offers to drive her home to Mr. Jairamdas's house in Begumganj and says she will tell Vasantlal today.

35.json.summary: Karuna's husband Aditya, a worker in the national movement, comes home after three years in jail. Their son Prakash was born three months after his arrest, and Karuna has lived through hunger by looking at the child. She expects a cheering crowd, but Aditya comes alone, a skeleton leaning on a stick; his comrades have forgotten him. He eats hungrily, collapses, and says he has tuberculosis. He asks whether his life deserves praise or regret; Karuna says it was a life like the gods', selfless and ideal. He dies. Karuna sells her jewellery, buys cows and lives by selling milk. At ten, Prakash mockingly puts chaff in a beggar woman's bag and says beggars should drown; at night he cries and says sorry, and Karuna feels Aditya is blessing him. But as he grows, his words and deeds differ. A brilliant student, he loves comfort and show. He pretends to be ill to avoid flood relief in Sindh, chooses a study trip to Ceylon over famine relief in Orissa, then goes to Kashmir. After coming first, he writes that he will serve the nation through education. Then he wins a government scholarship to England and plans to join the civil service. Karuna says magistrates punish patriots, and an Indian magistrate's sentence killed his father; she begs him not to take a government post. He refuses the scholarship but sulks for a month. When she tells him to go, he coldly says it is too late. She travels to the registrar and brings back the scholarship letter. She spends everything and borrows for his trip, and ages fast, but he does not notice. On the day he leaves, she angrily throws out all of Aditya's things and his picture. As Prakash goes, she sees a vision of Aditya holding Prakash's lifeless body, and faints. Afterwards she feeds the neighbourhood children, dogs, cats and birds. When Prakash's letter comes, she tears it up, then spends three days piecing it together. Dozing, she dreams that Prakash is a judge and Aditya is brought before him in chains. She burns the letter. In the morning she is found dead, Aditya's picture pressed to her heart, while Prakash's ship sails to Europe.

36.json.summary: Miss Padma is young, beautiful and clever. After an M.A. and a law degree she builds a practice that sometimes earns over a thousand rupees a month, ahead of the young male lawyers. She thinks marriage an unnatural bond and wants to enjoy life freely. She has many admirers, but they only want pleasure, and she feels an emptiness; what she really wants is someone's complete devotion. She loves Mr. Prasad, a handsome, learned college professor who also believes in free love and cannot be tied down. One evening she asks him to live in her bungalow. Prasad says it would end in jealousy, since each would keep other lovers. They agree to belong only to each other while staying free in all else. Prasad warns that if she breaks the promise he would want to disgrace or even kill her, and says he will live there as master, not guest. Padma happily agrees. Prasad earns only two hundred rupees a month but now spends freely on her money, keeps his own car and servants, and drinks day and night. The more Padma gives in, the more he controls her. After two years she is pregnant and has lost her fresh looks, and Prasad starts coming home late, going out with a college girl. One night Padma waits until one o'clock and questions him. He threatens to leave at once, and she ends up begging for a little kindness and weeping. He is out every evening near the birth and absent when she has a son. When she leaves the delivery room after five days, she learns he has taken from the bank all twenty thousand rupees she had saved for the child and gone to England with a college girl. In a rage she tramples his photo, burns his things and spits on his name. A month later, holding her baby at her gate, she watches a European couple walk by pushing their child in a pram, and her eyes fill with tears.

37.json.summary: The narrator, a poor writer of novels, is invited by the district magistrate, a cultured officer known for studying history and old coins, to visit his bungalow. The narrator dislikes Indians who flatter officials, and his friends advise him to refuse, saying the officer should have come himself, and telling funny stories about proud Indian officers. But he thinks it rude to refuse a polite invitation, and is also glad the officer did not see his poor, plain home. He goes, chats for a while, returns, and tells no one. Still, word spreads that the magistrate is his close friend and writes no report without his advice. Many people bring him complaints against the police, tax officers and their own offices, but he tells each that it is none of his business. One day Baldev Singh arrives, a big, strong childhood classmate whom the narrator taught at the village school some forty-five years ago. Baldev, now a landowner, praises him warmly, then explains that a police inspector who had quarrelled with his eldest son, a young wrestler, has framed him in a robbery case. The case is before a Deputy who is the inspector's close friend, so the son is sure to be punished, and the women at home have stopped eating. He begs the narrator to tell the magistrate the case is false, ask him to look into it himself, and say that Baldev is his brother. To get rid of him, the narrator promises, warning that officers usually back their own men, but he never means to say anything and soon forgets the matter. Some days later Baldev returns with his son, who touches the narrator's feet. The son has been fully cleared: the magistrate scolded the inspector for harassing decent people and warned he would be dismissed for another false case. Baldev thanks the narrator for saving four lives with his recommendation, saying that though people called him cold and unhelpful, his heart had told him his old friend would help.

38.json.summary: The narrator is a Brahmin priest, a Shastri, who loves the rich meals his wealthy clients give him. One morning, after his bath and prayers, he sets out in his clean yellow dhoti with his almanac and a thick stick to fix a wedding date at a client's house, hoping for a rupee and a good meal. It rained the night before and the road has pools of water. A motor car rushes past and splashes mud all over his face and clothes. People on the road clap and laugh at him. He cannot go to the client like this, and home is a mile away. Angry, he collects ten or twelve stones and waits. Soon the same car comes back with its owner, a sahib, and his wife. The priest throws stones, knocks off the sahib's hat, breaks the window and cuts his cheek. The sahib gets out and threatens to call the police, so the priest throws him into the mud and beats him. The wife, in high heels and silk sari, hits him with her umbrella; he takes it away. The sahib kicks him, and the priest knocks him down with his stick, and also beats the driver. About fifty people gather. The sahib begs not to be hurt and promises not to go to the police. The crowd says car owners splash people on purpose and laugh, and suggests punishments. The priest orders the sahib and the driver to do a hundred sit-ups while holding their ears, and tells the wife to count. The sahib refuses until the crowd starts pushing his car off the high road; then he begs and starts the sit-ups. The wife at first refuses to count. When another car appears, the sahib rubs his nose on the ground and promises never to ride in a car again. The priest says he may ride, but must treat people as human beings. The crowd stops the next two cars; the priest pulls one driver's ears and slaps both drivers, warning them not to splash people. Then someone shouts that the police are coming. Everyone runs, and the priest slips away into a lane and disappears.

39.json.summary: Pandit Chokhelal Sharma edits a famous magazine, 'Navras'. Since his wife died, he has become very fond of women. He throws good articles by men into the waste basket but accepts every piece sent by a woman, however weak, and writes back with high praise and a wish to meet her. Women writers turned away by other editors are delighted. Sales grow, letters of thanks pour in, and women ask him for blessings and advice. Every month a few visit him; he meets them at the station, keeps them a day or two and takes them to the cinema on free passes. They send him pickles and sweets, mend his clothes and cook for him, and people say he has grown very close to some of them. One day he receives a passionate, almost indecent love poem signed 'Kamakshi', in beautiful handwriting. He imagines a young, lovely woman and writes her a burning letter begging to meet her. She names the day she will come. He shaves, dresses in fine clothes, decorates the office with flowers and pretends to be deep in a book when she enters. But Kamakshi is a dark, fat, middle-aged woman, and his excitement dies. He says he is overworked and has a headache. She puts down a huge bundle of her poems and says she will stay a few days to nurse him and help with the magazine. Inside he curses her and her poetry; aloud he says her friend must be waiting. She reads her poems aloud without asking, and he feels as if he is being beaten with wet shoes. When she wants to read her play tomorrow, he says he is going to Prayag and does not know when he will return, then talks on the telephone for so long that after half an hour she leaves, promising to come again. He throws her bundle into the waste paper, calls her shameless, and orders the manager to take her poem out of the issue, even though the pages are already on the printing machine.

40.json.summary: The narrator, a poor school teacher, tells this story about his friend and neighbour Vikram. When lottery tickets go on sale, Vikram's father, uncle, mother and elder brother Prakash each buy one. Vikram dreams of travelling the world and building a great library, and will not depend on his family, so he and the narrator sell their old school books and buy a ten-rupee ticket together. The prize is ten lakh rupees, five for each. The ticket is in Vikram's name, with nothing written down. They keep it secret, but Vikram's young sister Kunti tells the whole house, and the family scolds them. Greed turns the whole family religious: the two Thakurs, once atheists, now bathe in the Ganga and pray, the mother fasts, and Prakash visits holy men. As the day nears, the narrator fears Vikram may deny his share. Vikram jokes that he might, and when the narrator asks for a written agreement, he refuses and they quarrel. Just then the two Thakurs, always as close as Ram and Lakshman, nearly come to blows over whether a prize won by anyone in the joint family must be shared. Prakash then comes home with a broken arm and bleeding head, happy: he had stood still while the holy man Jhakkar Baba stoned him, which is believed to make one's wish come true. He frightens his uncle out of trying it. On result day, 20 July, the family prays in the temple while Vikram goes to the post office. He returns smiling, and everyone rushes to him shouting praises to the gods. Then he announces that the prize went to a black man in America. The elder Thakur sacks the temple priest, the younger one sits down broken, Prakash takes a stick to beat Jhakkar Baba, and no one eats that night. Vikram takes the narrator to a hotel and says he laughed because the huge crowd at the post office showed how foolish their hopes were. When the narrator asks whether his intentions had truly turned dishonest, Vikram smiles and says to leave the curtain drawn.

41.json.summary: The narrator, Krishna, tells his own story ten years later. His mother is dead and his father is a doctor in Agra, so Krishna grows up in Lucknow with his rich, childless uncle, a lawyer, and his loving aunt. Next door lives Vimal Babu, a railway officer, whose little daughter Tara becomes Krishna's playmate. The aunt often says Tara will be her daughter-in-law, and both families take the marriage as settled. Later Krishna studies in Agra but spends every holiday in Lucknow, and the two grow into young people who love each other purely. After his exams Krishna becomes a sergeant in the army, posted in Lucknow. Then a rich man of the city, Chaudhari Sahib, offers his uncle a dowry of 8,000 rupees for Krishna. The greedy uncle says the talk of Tara was only a joke and asks Vimal Babu for six or seven thousand. Vimal Babu cannot pay, calls him a slave of money, and they quarrel. Krishna is angry but too timid to face his uncle. His father writes that he must obey the uncle. Krishna starts towards Tara's house but turns back from shame and fear, and Tara does not write. When his uncle calls him to meet Rai Sahib Sitaram, the rich man who wants him as a son-in-law, and says he has given his word, Krishna refuses to marry for money and breaks with him. His regiment is sent to Dehradun. Within a week a letter comes from Tara: her marriage has been fixed for the next day, she asks him to forgive her and not to forget her. Refused leave, he goes to Lucknow anyway. From the roof where they used to meet, he weeps and watches the wedding. Tara's mother sees him and says they would have waited if he had written even one line; Tara had watched for the postman all day. He refuses to see Tara and leaves. Dismissed from the army, he drifts for ten years, poor and joyless. Some years later Tara's husband invites him. Tara is happy and well, which hurts him. But her husband tells him that Tara still remembers him with love, treasures those days, and says she has found her Krishna in her husband. Krishna says that is enough for him.

42.json.summary: Dayakrishna returns from his new business in Calcutta because Leela, wife of his close friend Singar Singh, has urgently called him. Singar's rich father has died, and Dayakrishna owes the family a great deal. He finds Singar, a Sikh, with his hair cut, dressed in silk and spending his inheritance on parties and drink until he passes out. Leela, thin and ill, says her husband stays out all night, is infatuated with a courtesan named Madhuri and has offered to marry her. She trusts only Dayakrishna to bring him back, and shy Dayakrishna, who quietly worships her, promises to help. To pull Singar away, Dayakrishna begins visiting Madhuri himself. Singar treats her as a thing he has bought; Dayakrishna is humble and gentle and asks for nothing. Madhuri, never respected before, truly falls in love with him. Jealous Singar sets thugs on Dayakrishna, and Madhuri begs them to spare him. One winter evening she asks Dayakrishna to run away with her.
