Pressed, he admits he came only to free Singar for Leela's sake. Madhuri says he loves Leela, which he angrily denies, then asks plainly whether he will give her shelter, promising to give up her trade and Singar. Poor and unable to fully trust a courtesan, he asks for time. Hurt, she tells him he still cannot believe a woman like her can love truly, orders him never to return and shuts herself away. Two days later Singar bursts into Dayakrishna's house looking for Madhuri, who has left town. Her letter says she is disgusted with her life and with the men who use women like her. A week of searching finds nothing. Heartbroken, Singar tells Leela to go to her parents while he goes away. Leela says she married him, not his wealth, and will stay with him whatever happens, and they embrace lovingly for the first time in months. Singar tells her that Dayakrishna, who refused Madhuri, has gone looking for her. Just then Dayakrishna bursts in, covered in dust, cries that Madhuri is no longer in this world, and breaks down weeping.

43.json.summary: The narrator, of Lucknow, tells of his close friend Devnath of Delhi, a generous, carefree man. When Devnath dies before forty, he leaves his wife Gopa nothing but the house and household goods, and one daughter, Sunni; two sons had died young. Gopa proudly refuses help and offers of marriage. She rents out part of the house. The narrator then goes abroad on business for two years. When he returns, he finds Gopa grown old with worry: the tenant has left, she has lived by selling her jewellery, and the house is already mortgaged to a moneylender. Her only care now is Sunni's marriage. She wants to marry Sunni to the son of Lala Madarilal, a rich retired engineer known for taking bribes, who says he wants no dowry. The narrator meets him, is charmed, and the wedding is fixed. For four months Gopa works herself to exhaustion, borrowing from the whole neighbourhood to give far more than she can afford, because she feels she must do what Devnath would have done. Sunni is married in June. That winter Gopa tells the narrator that Sunni's husband, Kedarnath, is a pleasure-seeker who wanders about at night, and that proud Sunni will not bow to him; she has returned all her jewellery and lives in a plain white sari. At Madarilal's house, Kedar seems polite and gentle, and Madarilal blames the spoiled pride of both, mostly the bride. Sunni, pale and thin, tells him she wants faithfulness in return for faithfulness and will not compromise. In May Gopa calls him urgently: Kedar has run away with an actress, stolen money by forging his father's signature, and told Sunni he will not return while she is there. Sunni has broken her bangles, wiped off her sindoor and quarrelled with everyone. When the narrator reaches Madarilal's house, he finds Sunni's body being carried out: she drowned in the Yamuna that morning. He goes with the funeral and returns late, fearing for Gopa. But Gopa is calm, even glad. She says Sunni left the world with her honour, that a woman without love is better dead, and that her tears will be tears of pride, not grief. The narrator goes to bed lighter in heart, though he wonders whether this calm is only another form of her great pain.

44.json.summary: Tulsi Mahto, a villager, loves his daughter Subhagi as much as his son Ramu. Subhagi is clever and hard-working, while Ramu is dull. At the age of eleven Subhagi becomes a widow, and the whole family weeps. When she grows up, people urge Tulsi to remarry her, which their caste allows, but Subhagi refuses; she says she will work hard and serve her parents. Ramu and his sharp-tongued wife resent her. Subhagi does all the work of the house and the fields and does not let her old parents lift a finger, and Ramu complains that she wants him to work while sparing them. After a quarrel Tulsi calls the village elders to divide the property. The kind village official Thakur Sajan Singh scolds Ramu, but Ramu insists on living apart. Subhagi offers to live alone so the family does not break up, but Tulsi refuses to leave her. After the split, Subhagi looks after her parents well; she saves money, buys a buffalo, and the house fills with good things, which makes Ramu jealous. Part of the text is missing here. When the story picks up again, Tulsi has died. Subhagi insists on doing his funeral rites in grand style, with a feast for the Brahmins of eight villages, to show her brother what she can do; the text later makes clear she borrowed money from Sajan Singh for this. Her mother Lakshmi, who had never eaten before her husband in fifty years, stops eating, falls ill and dies on the fifteenth day. At the end she drives Ramu away and blesses Subhagi, asking her to do the last rites. Subhagi now owes Sajan Singh about 500 rupees, 300 for her father's rites and 200 for her mother's. For three years she works day and night, in the fields by day and grinding flour at night, and pays him 15 rupees every month without fail. Many marriage offers come, but she says the time has not come. On the day she pays the last instalment, Sajan Singh asks her to marry his son and become his daughter-in-law; he says he believed in caste, but she has broken all his barriers. Subhagi, who sees him as a father, accepts, and he blesses her.

45.json.summary: Two real sisters, Rampyari (Pyari) and Ramdulari (Dulari), are married to two brothers, Birju and Mathura, the sons of old Shivdas, a careful and money-minded village headman. When Birju dies, Shivdas, wanting to ease the young widow's grief, throws the key of the storeroom in front of Pyari and makes her the mistress of the house, while he himself takes up Birju's plough. Alone, Pyari opens the storeroom, which no one but Shivdas had ever entered, and sits among the grain, pots and papers. She comes out a changed woman. Once known for giving things away freely, she now refuses to lend a neighbour, Jhuniya, even one rupee. She runs the house with great skill: the food, milk and ghee improve, and everyone works harder. But she gives herself no rest and no comfort, and the others resent her. She has Dulari's bangles remade, and is moved to tears seeing Dulari and Mathura happy together. To keep up the family's name in the village, she slowly pawns or spends her own jewellery. When Dulari has a son, Pyari holds a grand celebration, and afterwards, pretending to sleep, she watches the parents loving their baby and hears Mathura say he pities her, since she has no one of her own. Shivdas dies, Dulari has two more children, and the farm does badly. Pyari works herself grey by thirty. Then Mathura decides to go to the east to earn better wages and takes Dulari and the children with him. Dulari does not want Pyari to come. Pyari cooks for them all night, gives advice about the children, and is left crying at the door. For days she lies in grief, and only the ploughman Jokhu, a lazy, hard-drinking man she often scolded, comforts her with real sympathy. Then she takes charge of the farm herself. Mathura sends no letters, but the melons and milk sell well, she gets back her pawned jewellery, dresses neatly and eats properly again. Jokhu, now trusted, works hard and with care. She feeds him dinner, teases him about getting married, and they argue over planting rice. When she presses him, he says he would marry only a woman just like her, calm, clever, thrifty and cheerful. Pyari blushes and says he is very naughty: he has said everything while joking.
